newsitem.title: USA: A look at virtual cash.
newsitem.headline: A look at virtual cash.

text.p: Several "virtual cash" options are already under way in the United States or set for release soon. Here's a thumbnail look at some of the major players:
WHO: CyberCash Inc., based in Reston, Va.

HOW IT WORKS: Shoppers download an "electronic wallet" from CyberCash's Web site or load it from a diskette. The wallets, offered by banks or CyberCash, hold information from one or more credit cards.

CyberCash technology links existing bank networks, merchants and customers. When a customer makes a purchase with an electronic wallet, the technology enables merchants to swiftly obtain bank authorisation for online purchases and issue electronic receipts.

CyberCash also offers CyberCoin, in which shoppers use their electronic wallets to make relatively small purchases of 25 cents to $10. Instead of a credit card, the amount is debited from a shopper's checking account, which is linked to the wallet through CyberCash technology.
COST: Free to shoppers. Banks, using technology licensed from CyberCash, charge merchants a fee for each transaction. CyberCash receives a small piece of the fee.
WEB SITE: http://www.cybercash.com

MERCHANTS: More than 200 participating merchants, including online software distributor Online Interactive, credit report company Maze.com and Worrble.com, an interactive word game. Hundreds more being evaluated or signing up.
BANKS: About 30.
WHEN: CyberCash service first offered in April 1995. CyberCoin launched last Sept. 30.
ON THE HORIZON: Electronic check service anticipated by end of 1997. Also working with banks in Canada, France and Germany.
WHO: Mark Twain Bank of St. Louis, licensing a system developed by Amsterdam, Netherlands-based, based DigiCash BV. A subsidiary of Mark Twain Bancshares.

HOW IT WORKS: After registering with the bank and sending a check to open an account, a shopper downloads and installs an "e-cash" wallet. Shoppers select passwords for making secure purchases and can transfer money from an e-cash "mint" at Mark Twain Bank to their computer hard drives for spending.
Customers can also transfer money to others with Mark Twain e-cash accounts.
COST: For shoppers, $11 setup fee, no transaction fee. Merchants pay a percentage of the purchase price on a sliding, negotiated scale similar to credit card arrangements.
WEB SITE: http://www.marktwain.com

MERCHANTS: About 300 participating merchants, 80 of them active, including the CDNow online music store, Community Connection, an Internet service provider in California; and the Libertarian Party of Virginia. One thousand more merchants expected in the next three months.
BANKS: None other directly involved.
WHEN: Service first offered in October 1995.
ON THE HORIZON: Alliance with one of three major online services, to be announced.
WHO: First Virtual Holdings Inc., based in San Diego.

HOW IT WORKS: Shoppers obtain a VirtualPIN (Virtual payment identification number) from First Virtual, which also holds shoppers' credit card information. Shoppers use the VirtualPIN to make purchases on the Internet. A purchase is confirmed with a buyer via e-mail from First Virtual before the transaction takes place via secure credit card networks not on the Internet.

COST: Buyers pay a $2 annual fee; sellers pay fees ranging from $10 for "pioneer sellers" to $350 for the first year and $250 per year thereafter if they want immediate settlements. For each transaction, sellers pay a 29-cent fee and 2 percent of the transaction price. Sellers also are charged a $1 settlement fee each time a payment is made to their bank account.
WEB SITE: http://www.fv.com
MERCHANTS: More than 2,700 participating merchants, including Apple Computer Inc., The Washington Weekly and the Farcast online news and information service.
BANKS: First USA Paymentech Inc. of Dallas handles merchant accounts
WHEN: Launched in October 1994.
ON THE HORIZON: First Virtual plans to announce new payment systems and technological advances in the coming months.
WHO: MasterCard and Visa's Secure Electronic Transactions, or SET.
HOW IT WORKS: Visa card or MasterCard holder uses an electronic wallet in conjunction with an Internet browser. The wallet contains a digital certificate with encrypted credit card information.

When customers order an item, they give a password. An exchange of electronic messages between the wallet and the merchant's computer follows. Once the merchant's computer has verified the information, it passes along the protected account information to the bank. The merchant never sees the credit card information. The wallet also verifies that the merchant can accept Mastercard or Visa transactions.
Once the purchase is authorised by the bank, the buyer gets confirmation of the purchase.

COST: Digital certificates obtained by shoppers from a bank or credit card issuer will vary in price and may be free under promotions in the initial rollout. Merchants pay $50 to $100 to sign up and a small percentage of each transaction, as is the case with conventional credit card purchases.
MERCHANTS: Up to 250 merchants in MasterCard's pilot programme, serving 25,000 to 50,000 cardholders
BANKS: Fifty to 100 banks in MasterCard's pilot programme by the end of the year.
WHEN: MasterCard pilot programme launched; full implementation expected in the second half of 1997. Visa plans test, pilot programme and full rollout as soon as software becomes available.
ON THE HORIZON: MasterCard plans SET-compliant chip card, as well as SET-modelled electronic debit transactions and funds transfers.
WHO: International Business Machines Corp., based in Armonk, N.Y.

HOW IT WORKS: IBM's InfoMarket service enables publishers and others to sell information -- including text, sound files and pictures -- in specially coded envelopes called cryptolope containers. Shoppers can read the description of the cryptolope container's contents but must obtain a key by registering online to open it.
When a customer opens a cryptolope container, it sends a signal to IBM, which notifies the publisher and sends a bill to the customer.
COST: Customer only pays for information contained in the cryptolope.
WEB SITES: http://www.infomarket.com
MERCHANTS: More than 6,800 magazines, 300 newspapers and 75 newswires.
BANKS: No banks involved.
WHEN: Available now.
ON THE HORIZON: More providers and more information, including credit reports, film clips, music, financial information, artwork, and more.
